title: finding(process): a dev-filed card whose report no current PM reads stays UNLABELLED forever — invisible to every sweep, and it caused a re-dispatch of work already done
body:
Filed by the `domain:ui` seat (session `session_012wwHa4aaFybxXrfmfHioDM`) after it **caused a concrete failure today**, not as a hypothetical. The failure is mine and is documented on #6318.

## What happened

I dispatched **#6318 bucket A** as a ~49-file corpus job needing per-group judgment. The lane came back with **no PR** and `needs_decision`:

> bucket A's per-group judgment was **ALREADY PERFORMED** on 2026-08-31 in the same run that landed bucket B. That run repaired 3 fixtures and reported **10 groups as forks**, filed as **#6939**, **#6940** and **#6942** — all still open and unassigned.

⇒ Every group in the remaining population was already escalated. The dispatch burned a full lane re-deriving a census that existed.

## ⭐ The mechanism, and why "read the comments" does not cover it

I *did* read #6318's comments — that is how I corrected an earlier wrong call on the same card. What I could not see is that **the three fork cards those comments name were, and had been for a day, completely unlabelled**:

| card | labels before today |
|---|---|
| #6939 (8 components / 20 files) | **none** |
| #6940 (data-table `rowActions` / 2 files) | **none** |
| #6942 (`TextSchema.variant` / 5 files) | **none** |

Three live decision cards — one of them carrying a fully-argued A/B/C recommendation — invisible to **every** label-based sweep: not in `pm:queue`, not in `needs-user-decision`, not in any `domain:*` view, not in the escalation list.

⚠️ **This is not a triage failure and not a dev failure.** The convention is correct and deliberate: a dev seat files **unlabelled** because grading and `domain:*` routing belong to triage — #6942's own body says so in its first line. The gap is structural:

> **A dev-filed card is graded when a PM reads the report that filed it. If no current PM ever reads that report, the card is never graded — and nothing else will ever surface it.**

#6939/#6940/#6942 were filed by a lane belonging to a **different session** on 2026-08-31. I took the seat afterwards. That report was never in my context, so the cards were never graded, so they existed only as issue numbers buried in a comment on their parent.

⇒ **The handover boundary is the failure surface.** Within a session the loop is closed by the PM reading its own lanes' reports; across sessions there is nothing.

## Scale — this is not one incident

Unlabelled live cards found and graded by this seat **today alone**, each discovered incidentally rather than by any sweep:

- **#6919** — found during a dedupe by an unrelated lane; a real card whose prohibition had been lifted by a landed PR, with no tracker for its remaining half.
- **#6939**, **#6940**, **#6942** — found only because a dispatch failed against them.

That is **four in one day**, all discovered by accident. ⛔ The number found by looking is zero, because there is no sweep that can look: an unlabelled card matches no label query, which is exactly what makes this class **self-concealing** — it generates no failed sweep, no stale-label report, and no signal at all. It is only ever found by tripping over it.

## What this cost, concretely

- One dev lane (~27 min) spent re-deriving a 28-file census that already existed.
- A PM dispatch order written against a population (**49 files, unjudged**) that had been **27 files, fully judged** for a day.
- #6939's own title says **24** where its table sums to **20** — a transcription error that has stood since filing because nobody graded the card and therefore nobody read it closely. *(Corrected additively by today's lane.)*

⚠️ And the near-miss: had bucket A genuinely been unjudged, the lane would have produced a correct PR and nobody would have learned the three cards were invisible.

## Options

- **A — a sweep for unlabelled open issues.** `is:issue is:open no:label` is one query. Cheapest possible instrument; catches the whole class by construction rather than by inference. ⛔ Its weakness is that it finds them only *after* filing, so a card can still sit unlabelled between sweeps.
- **B — make grading part of filing.** A dev seat applies a provisional `pm:untriaged` (or similar) so the card is at least *findable*, with triage still owning the real grade. Trades a small convention change for making the class impossible.
- **C — make the PM's report-handling explicitly include grading every card the report filed**, and make an unread predecessor report a handover item. Addresses the session boundary directly, but relies on a discipline that has already failed once.

**Recommendation: A now, B next.** A is a single query that could be run today and would have surfaced all four of today's cards immediately. B removes the failure mode rather than detecting it, and costs one line in the dev-filing convention. ⛔ C alone is insufficient — it asks a human-shaped process to be reliable where a query would be exact.

## What this card does NOT claim

- ⛔ Not that the unlabelled-filing convention is wrong. It is right: a dev seat should not grade its own findings.
- ⛔ Not that triage failed. These cards were never routed to triage's attention by anything.
- ⛔ Not that all four were high priority. #6942 is p2. The point is **not their severity but their invisibility** — and that one of them was load-bearing for a dispatch I actually made.

Related: **#6853** (cards that read dispatchable but are not — the same family, different mechanism: there the body misleads, here there is nothing to read at all) · **#6653** / **#7041** (machine-findable unblock conditions on *blocked* cards; this is the same argument for *ungraded* ones) · #6318 (where it fired) · #6919, #6939, #6940, #6942 (the four instances).
